[[](https://www.instagram.com/playfulheartparenting) playfulheartp... 652K There will inevitably be comments/criticism that I was dismissing his emotions here, but I do not see it that way, and here’s why: At the time, he was three and it was lots of meltdowns throughout the day. We were learning to navigate these together and not every single one could be a sit down and talk about it thing. In this moment, I was actually SUPER HUNGRY too — hence the face-stuffing in this clip. We’d just gotten back from a walk where I pushed the double stroller uphill in the hot sun while wearing my baby in the carrier. I was sweaty. I was tired. I was sliding toward hangry. 😮‍💨 Then he plopped down and started making whining, grunting sounds. So, 1️⃣: I needed a playful buffer to stabilize MY mood; I knew I’d be better with a little food — hey, that rhymed! Reason 2️⃣: He was in a funk - and 3 at the time (reasoning/talking through it was not helpful in the heat of the moment). So asking what was wrong wasn’t getting us anywhere. I tried asking if the grumpy fairy had sprinkled grumpy dust on him. 🧚 He did not like that. Just furrowed his brow and grunted louder. So I pivoted. I tried the moose thing. And he did that cute toddler thing — you know, where they’re trying not to smile but can’t help it? For whatever reason, the moose was a hit. And it did the two things we needed: 1 — It relaxed him enough to tell me what he needed 2 — It kept me from snapping or grumbling back (long enough to eat a few bites and feel human again) Now, if it had made him more upset or he’d said Stop!! I would have simply stopped right away! But in this instance, it was exactly what we both needed. A little humor to get us on the same page. 💞 Btw I have an audio course called **Activate Play Mode** where we dive into the underlying strategies that help you do this kind of pivoting — on the fly, even if you’re hangry, tired, or wildly unmotivated.

[[](https://www.instagram.com/playfulheartparenting) playfulheartp... 652K There will inevitably be comments/criticism that I was dismissing his emotions here, but I do not see it that way, and here’s why: At the time, he was three and it was lots of meltdowns throughout the day. We were learning to navigate these together and not every single one could be a sit down and talk about it thing. In this moment, I was actually SUPER HUNGRY too — hence the face-stuffing in this clip. We’d just gotten back from a walk where I pushed the double stroller uphill in the hot sun while wearing my baby in the carrier. I was sweaty. I was tired. I was sliding toward hangry. 😮‍💨 Then he plopped down and started making whining, grunting sounds. So, 1️⃣: I needed a playful buffer to stabilize MY mood; I knew I’d be better with a little food — hey, that rhymed! Reason 2️⃣: He was in a funk - and 3 at the time (reasoning/talking through it was not helpful in the heat of the moment). So asking what was wrong wasn’t getting us anywhere. I tried asking if the grumpy fairy had sprinkled grumpy dust on him. 🧚 He did not like that. Just furrowed his brow and grunted louder. So I pivoted. I tried the moose thing. And he did that cute toddler thing — you know, where they’re trying not to smile but can’t help it? For whatever reason, the moose was a hit. And it did the two things we needed: 1 — It relaxed him enough to tell me what he needed 2 — It kept me from snapping or grumbling back (long enough to eat a few bites and feel human again) Now, if it had made him more upset or he’d said Stop!! I would have simply stopped right away! But in this instance, it was exactly what we both needed. A little humor to get us on the same page. 💞 Btw I have an audio course called **Activate Play Mode** where we dive into the underlying strategies that help you do this kind of pivoting — on the fly, even if you’re hangry, tired, or wildly unmotivated.

We’d just gotten back from a walk where I pushed the double stroller uphill in the hot sun while wearing my baby in the carrier. I was sweaty. I was tired. I was sliding toward hangry. 😮‍💨 Then he plopped down and started making whining, grunting sounds. So, 1️⃣: I needed a playful buffer to stabilize MY mood; I knew I’d be better with a little food — hey, that rhymed! Reason 2️⃣: He was in a funk - and 3 at the time (reasoning/talking through it was not helpful in the heat of the moment). So asking what was wrong wasn’t getting us anywhere. I tried asking if the grumpy fairy had sprinkled grumpy dust on him. 🧚 He did not like that. Just furrowed his brow and grunted louder. So I pivoted. I tried the moose thing. And he did that cute toddler thing — you know, where they’re trying not to smile but can’t help it? For whatever reason, the moose was a hit. And it did the two things we needed: 1 — It relaxed him enough to tell me what he needed 2 — It kept me from snapping or grumbling back (long enough to eat a few bites and feel human again) Now, if it had made him more upset or he’d said Stop!! I would have simply stopped right away! But in this instance, it was exactly what we both needed. [[](https://www.instagram.com/playfulheartparenting) playfulheartp... 652K There will inevitably be comments/criticism that I was dismissing his emotions here, but I do not see it that way, and here’s why: At the time, he was three and it was lots of meltdowns throughout the day. We were learning to navigate these together and not every single one could be a sit down and talk about it thing. In this moment, I was actually SUPER HUNGRY too — hence the face-stuffing in this clip. We’d just gotten back from a walk where I pushed the double stroller uphill in the hot sun while wearing my baby in the carrier. I was sweaty. I was tired. I was sliding toward hangry. 😮‍💨 Then he plopped down and started making whining, grunting sounds. So, 1️⃣: I needed a playful buffer to stabilize MY mood; I knew I’d be better with a little food — hey, that rhymed! Reason 2️⃣: He was in a funk - and 3 at the time (reasoning/talking through it was not helpful in the heat of the moment). So asking what was wrong wasn’t getting us anywhere. I tried asking if the grumpy fairy had sprinkled grumpy dust on him. 🧚 He did not like that. Just furrowed his brow and grunted louder. So I pivoted. I tried the moose thing. And he did that cute toddler thing — you know, where they’re trying not to smile but can’t help it? For whatever reason, the moose was a hit. And it did the two things we needed: 1 — It relaxed him enough to tell me what he needed 2 — It kept me from snapping or grumbling back (long enough to eat a few bites and feel human again) Now, if it had made him more upset or he’d said Stop!! I would have simply stopped right away! But in this instance, it was exactly what we both needed. A little humor to get us on the same page. 💞 Btw I have an audio course called **Activate Play Mode** where we dive into the underlying strategies that help you do this kind of pivoting — on the fly, even if you’re hangry, tired, or wildly unmotivated.
